title: Veneto - The Spirit of Venice
quiz.0.question: Which grape is Prosecco mainly made from?
quiz.0.explanation: Prosecco must be made from at least 85% Glera.
quiz.1.question: What does Amarone’s appassimento process mean?
quiz.1.explanation: Appassimento means laying whole bunches on racks in ventilated lofts and drying them for at least 3-4 months to concentrate sugars and extract.
quiz.2.question: What is the minimum alcohol for Amarone della Valpolicella?
quiz.2.explanation: Amarone has a legal minimum of 14% ABV, and wines often reach 15-16% or more; it must age at least 2 years, Riserva 4.
quiz.3.question: Which white grape is Soave mainly made from?
quiz.3.explanation: Soave must be made from at least 70% Garganega.
slides.0.title: 🍷 Veneto
slides.0.subtitle: A wine kingdom with the spirit of Venice
slides.1.title: 📍 Region Overview
slides.1.content:
Veneto is the largest and most populous of the “Tre Venezie” (Veneto, Trentino-Alto Adige and Friuli Venezia Giulia), with Venice as its capital. It is Italy’s third-largest region by vineyard area (about 80,000 ha, after Sicilia and Puglia) and, as of 2017, has 14 DOCGs and 29 DOCs; it leads Italy in DOC/G output (over 50% of production is DOC/G, with IGT about 25-30%).

📍
Location
The Alps (the Dolomites and the Venetian Prealps) to the north, the Adriatic to the south-east, the Padana plain to the south and Lake Garda to the west
🌾
Vineyards
About 80,000 ha; Verona is the most productive province (about 40% of the region), followed by Treviso
🏆
Appellations
14 DOCGs + 29 DOCs; second in Italy for number of DOCGs (after Piemonte)
🍾
Industry
Verona hosts Vinitaly; the Conegliano school of oenology, founded in 1876, is one of Italy’s first and most important wine schools
slides.2.title: 🏛 History and Cultural Heritage
slides.2.content:
From Roman “Retico” to UNESCO World Heritage in 2019 — the Venetian Republic’s thousand years of sea trade fostered a commercial outlook open to foreign grapes

Roman era
Retico and Acinatico: Valpolicella, once called “Retico”, was prized in Roman times; the ancient wines Retico and Acinatico are seen as forerunners of today’s sweet recioto from Verona province
13th-14th c.
Venice in its prime: the Venetian Republic extended over Veneto, Friuli and part of Lombardia, and viticulture and trade flourished in the 13th-14th centuries; Garganega is documented from the 13th century
1797-1876
Turning points: Napoléon occupied Veneto in 1797, ending more than a thousand years of Venetian independence; Austrian rule followed until Veneto joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866; the Conegliano school of oenology, founded in 1876, launched the industry’s recovery
2019
UNESCO World Heritage: the Prosecco hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene were inscribed as a World Heritage Site
9th c. BC
The Veneti already settled
1797

slides.3.title: 📜 Veneto’s History: From the Veneti to the Venetian Republic (IWS)
slides.3.content:
The Veneti and the Romans

It is certain that the Veneti had settled in Veneto by the 9th century BC, learning viticulture and winemaking from the neighbouring Rhaeti and Etruscans (legend says the Veneti came from Anatolia after the fall of Troy, but there is no archaeological evidence). The Veneti allied with Rome against Celtic invasions, and in 49 BC Caesar granted them Roman citizenship; the Romans then expanded the vineyards and raised output, and the ancient local wines “Retico” and “Acinatico” are seen as the forerunners of today’s sweet recioto from Verona province.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire (5th century), the Lombards crossed the Alps in 568 and Veneto split into an inland part (under the Lombards) and a coastal part (under Byzantium); viticulture declined sharply until Venice rose as a maritime power. Venice became independent of Byzantium in the 9th century as a republic led by an elected “Doge”, later extending its power over Veneto, Friuli, part of Lombardia and parts of today’s Slovenia and Croatia

From Venice’s decline to Italian unification

In the 17th century the rise of the Ottoman Empire, new sea routes and the discovery of the Americas undermined Venice, and the severe winter of 1709 devastated viticulture (many vines froze to death). In 1797 Napoléon occupied Veneto, ending more than a thousand years of Venetian independence; after his defeat Austria took control, and Veneto only joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866
In 1876 the Conegliano school of oenology (Scuola Enologica di Conegliano) was founded — one of Italy’s first and most important wine schools — with early work on fighting oidium, phylloxera and downy mildew, marking the start of the industry’s recovery

Two world wars and the post-war boom

Veneto was a main battlefield in World War I, and destruction and poverty drove mass emigration; World War II caused further damage, and real economic recovery only began in the 1960s, when small businesses in furniture, leather, textiles and metalwork flourished and made Veneto one of the richest regions in Italy and Europe; the wine industry modernised alongside, and the international success of Soave and Valpolicella made Veneto one of Europe’s largest wine regions
💡 Ups and downs: Valpolicella and Soave were internationally famous in the 1970s-80s, then slid into mediocrity as demand outstripped supply; in the 1990s the same appellations led a quality revival, and today the industry combines large volumes of affordable wine with a premium path focused on native grapes, terroir and single vineyards (cru)
slides.4.title: 🌍 Terroir
slides.4.content:
The overall climate is mild continental: the Alps block cold northerly winds and trap warm air from the south, while the Adriatic and Lake Garda moderate temperatures; the further from the sea and the lake, the more continental it becomes

🏔️

The hills

Where: along the Prealps from Lake Garda north-east to the Friuli border, plus the Colli Berici and Colli Euganei in the centre

Share: 15% of the region’s area but nearly 40% of its vineyards

Climate: semi-continental with wide day-night swings that preserve aromatic complexity and acidity; up to 900-1,250 mm of rain a year

Appellations: Bardolino, Valpolicella, Soave, Conegliano Valdobbiadene

🌾

The plains and coastal plain

Share: 56% of the area, with nearly 60% of the vineyards on the plains

Rivers: the Brenta, Piave, Livenza, Tagliamento, Adige and Po flow across them to the Adriatic

Climate: hot, humid summers and cold, damp winters with frequent fog; the coast, moderated by the Adriatic, is mildest

Rainfall: lowest on the plains and coast, 500-900 mm a year

🗺️ Veneto’s three sub-regions

Western Veneto
Verona province
Bardolino, Valpolicella, Soave
Central Veneto
Vicenza and Padova provinces
Gambellara, Breganze, Colli Euganei
Eastern Veneto
Treviso and Venezia provinces
Conegliano Valdobbiadene, Piave
The Alps
30% of the area
Only about 2% planted to vines
slides.5.title: 🧬 The Native Grapes
slides.5.content:
🔴 Corvina (Corvina Veronese) — the heart of Valpolicella

Traits: late-budding, mid-late ripening and thick-skinned, ideal for appassimento

Style: medium colour, bright acidity, light to medium tannin and body

Aromas: sour cherry, violet, herbs, bitter almond

Rules: Valpolicella needs Corvina 45-95% (up to 50% of which may be Corvinone) and Rondinella 5-30%

⚪ Garganega — the soul of Soave

Identity: one of Italy’s oldest grapes, the same variety as Sicilia’s Grecanico Dorato

Traits: late-ripening, vigorous and productive; vigour and yields must be controlled to bring out its delicate semi-aromatic character

Aromas: white flowers, citrus, ripe yellow fruit, almond, minerality

Soave rules: at least 70%, with up to 30% Trebbiano di Soave and/or Chardonnay

🥂 Glera — the core of Prosecco

Identity: originally called Prosecco (more precisely Prosecco Tondo), of uncertain origin

Traits: late-ripening and semi-aromatic, prone to fungal disease; grown mainly in Treviso province

Aromas: white flowers, lemon, pear, apple, peach; neutral when high-yielding on the flat, deeper on sunny, low-yielding slopes

Plantings: Veneto’s most planted grape (28%)
slides.6.title: 🍇 Veneto Plantings and More Native Grapes (IWS)
slides.6.content:
Plantings (Regione Veneto, 2013)

Glera 28% · Garganega 13% · Pinot Grigio 12% · Merlot 9% · Corvina 8% · Cabernet Sauvignon 4% · Chardonnay 4% · Rondinella 3% · Cabernet Franc 3% · Corvinone 1% · Pinot Bianco 1% · Others 14%. The natives Glera, Garganega and Corvina Veronese make up nearly half the plantings, and over 60% are native or Italian grapes.

🍷 A Merlot kingdom: Bordeaux grapes arrived in central and eastern Veneto in the 1830s and grew in importance after phylloxera; with nearly 200 years of history they are considered traditional (often blended and labelled simply “Cabernet”). Merlot is now the region’s most planted red and Veneto has Italy’s largest Merlot plantings; Cabernet Franc was historically more widespread but has been overtaken by Cabernet Sauvignon

Valpolicella’s supporting grapes

Rondinella: grown in Verona province for centuries but only documented in the late 19th century, and proven to be an offspring of Corvina. Easy to grow, disease-, cold- and drought-resistant and productive; its resistance to fungal disease suits appassimento. Cherry aromas, low tannin and light body, but without Corvina’s character and elegance
Corvinone: native to Verona and once thought to be a clone of Corvina, but DNA shows they are unrelated; the name means “big Corvina”. More tannic than Corvina, it adds structure, body and savoury notes after appassimento; it is now an official grape, though its share is limited
Molinara: named after “mulino” (mill) for the flour-like bloom on its berries. Once a classic part of Valpolicella, it was removed from the required grapes in 2003, though some estates still feel it balances the richness of Amarone and adds acidity
Oseleta: an ancient Verona native, nearly extinct by the 1970s because of its low, irregular yields; rediscovered and revived by Masi in the 1980s, small amounts add structure to blends and it is increasingly used in Valpolicella

Raboso Piave and other key natives

Raboso Piave: very high in tannin and acidity, native to the Piave alluvial plain; the name may come from “rabbioso” (furious), describing its rustic style. It lost ground to Merlot from the 1950s but has been revived by local producers since the 1980s; fully ripe fruit with enough oak and bottle age tames it, giving deep-coloured wines with berries, violet, tobacco and leather
Vespaiola: an ancient grape found only in Vicenza province, named after “vespe” (wasps) that love its sweet fruit. Vigorous and high in acidity, it is best known for sweet passito (Breganze’s Torcolato)
Durella: native to the Monti Lessini; its high acidity makes it ideal for sparkling wine (Lessini Durello DOC), crisp with mineral and flinty notes
Manzoni Bianco: a crossing bred in the 1930s by Luigi Manzoni of the Conegliano school (originally Incrocio Manzoni 6.0.13), long thought to be Riesling × Pinot Bianco though recent research suggests Riesling × Chardonnay; fresh, delicately aromatic, mineral and spicy
slides.7.title: ✨ The Three Star Wines
slides.7.content:
Veneto’s three international stars, representing sparkling, red and white

🥂 Prosecco DOC / DOCG

Mainly Glera, with a second fermentation in tank (Charmat method) to keep fresh fruit. Light, soft and refreshing, with white flowers, lemon, pear, apple and peach. The best come from the hill DOCGs of Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo.

🍷 Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG

Essentially a “dry Recioto”: made from dried grapes fermented to almost no residual sugar. At least 14% ABV and 2 years’ ageing (Riserva 4); often 15-16% or more. Ripe berries, dried fruit, tobacco, liquorice, dark chocolate, leather.

🤍 Soave Classico DOC

At least 70% Garganega, from the historic hills between Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone. Firm acidity and a rich body, with chamomile, iris, citrus and almond, and more ageing potential than expected. The stricter tier is Soave Superiore DOCG.
slides.8.title: 🏞️ Bardolino & Custoza: Fresh Wines from Lake Garda (IWS)
slides.8.content:
Bardolino — light reds from the “Olive Riviera”

On the south-eastern shore of Lake Garda, the “Riviera degli Ulivi” (Olive Riviera), vineyards share the land with olive trees, and only light rosso and rosato wines are made. The blend is led by Corvina Veronese (35-80% by law, about 60% on average), with Rondinella (10-40%) and Molinara (0-15%). The wines are pale ruby, light and fresh, with flowers, pink grapefruit, cherry and wild berries; drink young and lightly chilled.

🏆 Categories: Bardolino DOC (including Bardolino Classico, Bardolino Chiaretto rosé and Bardolino Novello) and Bardolino Superiore DOCG (lower yields, higher alcohol, at least 1 year of ageing). The best come from the classico zone (Bardolino and surrounding villages), with a distinctive savoury (salato) character

Custoza DOC (Bianco di Custoza)

A white-wine zone named after the hamlet of Custoza, overlapping the southern part of Bardolino DOC, on gravelly morainic soils. The blend: Trebbiano Toscano, Garganega, Tai and Cortese, with Trebbiano Toscano 10-45% and Garganega 20-40% by law, and quality producers favouring more Garganega. Pale, light-bodied and clean, it is one of Italy’s best-value whites
💡 Lugana DOC in brief: an inter-regional appellation based on Turbiana, mostly in Lombardia, though about 60% of the wine is bottled by producers on the Veneto side (around Peschiera del Garda, notably San Benedetto di Lugana)

slides.10.title: 🌬️ Appassimento in Depth
slides.10.content:
Appassimento (drying) is Valpolicella’s most distinctive tradition: healthy, fully ripe whole bunches are dried for months to concentrate sugars and extract

🌿 Traditional fruttai

Racks: traditional wooden or bamboo “arele” or “graticci”, with grapes in a single layer

Where: well-ventilated hillside lofts called “fruttai”

Time: at least 3-4 months, sometimes longer

Risk: grey rot must be avoided

Noble rot: a little can add glycerol and layers of flavour, though producers disagree

⚙️ Modern practice

Containers: wooden or plastic crates are also used

Rules: no vinification before 1 December of the year after harvest

Yield: only 65% of the harvest per hectare may be used for Amarone or Recioto

Ageing: Amarone at least 2 years, Riserva 4; traditionally in large neutral Slavonian oak, now sometimes in new small barrels

The botrytis debate: some producers avoid it, believing it lowers tannin and acidity and shortens ageing potential

The same dried grapes, three results

🍬 Recioto

Fermentation is stopped by chilling once the desired sweetness is reached, keeping residual sugar

Traditionally Valpolicella’s most prized wine

🍷 Amarone

Usually dried for a shorter time and fermented until the sugar is almost fully converted

“Amaro” means bitter — slightly bitter compared with Recioto

🌿 Ripasso

Fresh Valpolicella is steeped on Amarone/Recioto pomace for 1-2 weeks, triggering a brief second fermentation

Revived by Masi in the 1960s

slides.12.title: 🥂 The Prosecco Hierarchy
slides.12.content:
From a local wine to a global phenomenon — in 2019 the Prosecco hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene became a UNESCO World Heritage Site

👑 Superiore di Cartizze
A small, famous steep hill in Valdobbiadene and the top sub-zone of Conegliano Valdobbiadene; often made in a slightly sweet Dry style
🏆 Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG
The historic core hills at the foot of the Prealps in Treviso province; “Rive” marks steep vineyards from a specific village or sub-area
⭐ Asolo Prosecco DOCG
Around the town of Asolo, slightly warmer and wetter than Conegliano Valdobbiadene, also based on Glera, with much smaller production
🥂 Prosecco DOC
A large inter-regional DOC across Veneto and Friuli, made in volume, fresh and easy

slides.14.title: 🍷 The Four Valpolicella Appellations
slides.14.content:
Same grapes, same area — Valpolicella has four official appellations, from light to rich

🍷 Valpolicella DOC (fresh and easy)

Made from fresh grapes. Sour cherry and flowers with a bitter-almond finish, light body, moderate alcohol, low tannin and bright acidity; Superiore must age at least 1 year.

🌿 Valpolicella Ripasso DOC (medium complexity)

Fresh Valpolicella is steeped on Amarone and/or Recioto pomace for 1-2 weeks, triggering a brief second fermentation; up to 15% fresh Amarone may be added. At least 1 year’s ageing before release; Superiore needs at least 13% ABV.

🏆 Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG (dry)

Dried grapes fermented to almost no residual sugar. At least 14% ABV and 2 years’ ageing; Riserva 4 years.

🍬 Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG — the original sweet style

Method
Dried grapes
At least 3-4 months
Difference
Fermentation stopped by chilling
Residual sugar kept
Aromas
Berries, dried fruit
Maraschino cherry, chocolate
Name
Dialect “recia” (ear)
Only berries from the bunch’s “shoulders”
slides.15.title: 🗺️ Other Key Appellations of Central and Eastern Veneto (IWS)
slides.15.content:
Gambellara — Soave’s “twin”

Another white-only DOC based on Garganega (at least 80%), right next to Soave’s eastern edge and entirely in Vicenza province, with volcanic basalt soils like eastern Soave. Recioto di Gambellara DOCG is a sweet passito from 100% Garganega (classico zone only), traditionally dried by the “picai” method (bunches tied with string and hung from rafters). Gambellara is also the only area in Veneto that makes Vin Santo

Breganze — a hidden gem championed by Maculan

At the foot of the Asiago plateau, known for fine Bordeaux blends and varietals. Its two distinctive wines are both made from the native white Vespaiola: Torcolato (a sweet passito from 100% Vespaiola, named after “torcolare”, the traditional twisting of bunches onto strings for drying) and Vespaiolo (a dry varietal white)

Colli Berici & Colli Euganei — limestone and volcanic hills

Colli Berici DOC: isolated hills of marine limestone south of Vicenza, best known for varietal Tai Rosso (Cannonau/Grenache), at its best in the central Barbarano sub-zone (100% Tai Rosso required)
Colli Euganei DOC: volcanic hills (basalt, tuff, rhyolite) that were among the first in Veneto to plant Cabernet and Merlot in the 19th century. Colli Euganei Fior d'Arancio DOCG is one of Italy’s few appellations for the rare Moscato Giallo, at its most typical as a rich passito

The eastern plains: Piave DOC and Lison-Pramaggiore

Piave DOC: a large appellation across Treviso and Venezia provinces and a major Merlot area; its most distinctive wine is Raboso del Piave DOC from the native Raboso Piave — deep-coloured, very tannic and high in acidity, with at least 2 years’ ageing required. Piave Malanotte (Malanotte del Piave) DOCG, once a special designation of Piave DOC, became its own DOCG; 15-30% of the grapes must undergo appassimento to tame Raboso’s fierce tannins
Lison-Pramaggiore DOC: straddling the Veneto/Friuli Venezia Giulia border, where Merlot and the two Cabernets are considered traditional. Lison DOCG, once the special designation for Tai (Friulano), was promoted to its own DOCG — the first DOCG in the world for Tai/Friulano

Asolo-Montello: the Prealpine hills beyond Conegliano

Asolo Prosecco DOCG: around the town of Asolo, slightly warmer and wetter than Conegliano Valdobbiadene, also based on Glera, with far smaller production than Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG. Montello (Montello Rosso) DOCG, created in 2011, is a Bordeaux-style red led by Cabernet Sauvignon (40-70%), with clay-rich slopes giving structured, age-worthy wines
slides.16.title: 🍽️ Food and Wine Pairing
slides.16.content:
Venetian food and wine — seafood from Venice, Verona’s braised meats and even Amarone used as an ingredient

🥂 Prosecco Brut DOCG

With: Sarde in saor (Venetian sweet-and-sour sardines)
One of Venice’s oldest dishes: sardines marinated with onions and vinegar, pine nuts and raisins. Prosecco’s fresh bubbles cut the oil and its floral notes balance the sweet and sour — a classic Venetian aperitif.

🤍 Soave Classico DOC

With: Baccalà alla vicentina (Vicenza-style salt cod)
Salt cod slowly cooked with milk and onions, the pride of Vicenza. Garganega’s minerality and almond-blossom notes suit the sweet flesh of the cod, and its acidity keeps it fresh.

🌿 Valpolicella Ripasso

With: Pasta e fagioli (pasta and bean soup)
A traditional Venetian peasant dish with a rich bean broth. Ripasso’s fruit and tannins match the hearty beans — warming and comforting.

🍷 Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG

With: Risotto all’Amarone
The ultimate match: a risotto made with Amarone, served with Amarone. Wine and dish from the same source, richness meeting richness.
slides.17.title: ⚖️ Amarone vs Valpolicella Superiore: Same Grapes, Different Methods
slides.17.description: Both come from Valpolicella and use the same grapes (mainly Corvina), but winemaking makes them worlds apart.
slides.17.pairs.0.title: Amarone vs Valpolicella Superiore — same grapes, different methods
slides.17.pairs.0.intro: Both come from Valpolicella and use the same grapes (mainly Corvina), but winemaking makes them worlds apart.
slides.17.pairs.0.left.name: Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG
slides.17.pairs.0.left.grape: Corvina 45-95% (up to 50% of which may be Corvinone), Rondinella 5-30%, others up to 25%
slides.17.pairs.0.left.soil: Valpolicella’s alluvial and morainic soils and limestone/marl, with volcanic basalt around Marano
slides.17.pairs.0.left.climate: Mild, sheltered by the Monti Lessini and moderated by Lake Garda
slides.17.pairs.0.left.elevation: South-facing terraces up to about 500 m
slides.17.pairs.0.left.style: Grapes dried for months after harvest (appassimento) and not vinified before 1 December of the following year; at least 14% ABV, often 15-16% or more, full-bodied yet almost dry
slides.17.pairs.0.left.aromas: Ripe berries, dried fruit, tobacco, liquorice, dark chocolate, coffee, leather, spice
slides.17.pairs.0.left.producers: Quintarelli, Romano dal Forno, Bertani, Masi, Allegrini
slides.17.pairs.0.right.name: Valpolicella Superiore DOC
slides.17.pairs.0.right.style: Made from selected fresh grapes, with better structure, higher alcohol and more concentration; some use ripasso or add some dried grapes
slides.17.pairs.0.right.aromas: Sour cherry, flowers, spice, a bitter-almond touch
slides.17.pairs.0.keyDifference: Winemaking is everything: Amarone uses grapes dried for months, with at least 14% ABV and 2 years’ ageing; Valpolicella Superiore uses fresh grapes and ages at least 1 year. Ripasso sits in between — Valpolicella is passed over Amarone or Recioto pomace for a brief second fermentation.

slides.22.title: 🎓 Key Takeaways
slides.22.points.0: ✓ Veneto is Italy’s third-largest region by vineyard area (about 80,000 ha), with 14 DOCGs and 29 DOCs and Italy’s largest DOC/G output; its capital is Venice
slides.22.points.1: ✓ The Venetian Republic’s thousand years of sea trade fostered a commercial outlook open to foreign grapes; the Conegliano school of oenology was founded in 1876
slides.22.points.2: ✓ Three sub-regions: the west (Verona: Bardolino, Valpolicella, Soave), the centre (Vicenza, Padova) and the east (Treviso, Venezia: Prosecco, Piave)
slides.22.points.3: ✓ The natives Glera (28%), Garganega (13%) and Corvina make up nearly half the plantings; Veneto also has Italy’s largest plantings of Merlot and Pinot Grigio
slides.22.points.4: ✓ Appassimento: grapes dry for at least 3-4 months and may not be vinified before 1 December of the following year; the same dried grapes make Recioto (sweet) or Amarone (dry)
slides.22.points.5: ✓ Amarone needs at least 14% ABV and 2 years’ ageing (Riserva 4); Ripasso passes Valpolicella over Amarone/Recioto pomace for a second fermentation
slides.22.points.6: ✓ Soave needs at least 70% Garganega; Soave Classico is a DOC, while Soave Superiore and Recioto di Soave are DOCGs
slides.22.points.7: ✓ Prosecco is Glera with a second fermentation in tank; the top tier is the Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo DOCGs, with Cartizze as the top sub-zone
slides.23.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
slides.23.questions.0.question: Which special technique is used for Amarone della Valpolicella?
slides.23.questions.0.explanation: Amarone is made by appassimento: whole bunches are laid in single layers in ventilated fruttai for at least 3-4 months and may not be vinified before 1 December of the following year; the wine is fermented almost dry, with at least 14% ABV.
slides.23.questions.1.question: What is the core grape of Prosecco?
slides.23.questions.1.explanation: Glera, whose original name was Prosecco, is the main Prosecco grape, grown mainly in Treviso province; Prosecco is made by second fermentation in tank to keep its fresh fruit.
slides.23.questions.2.question: Which statements about Prosecco are correct? (multiple choice)
slides.23.questions.2.options.0: A. It is made by the Charmat (tank) method
slides.23.questions.2.options.1: B. It comes mainly from Veneto and Friuli
slides.23.questions.2.options.2: C. Like Champagne, it uses the traditional method (second fermentation in bottle)
slides.23.questions.2.options.3: D. Its main grape is Glera
slides.23.questions.2.explanation: Prosecco undergoes its second fermentation in large steel tanks, which costs less than the Champagne method and gives a fresh, fruity style. It comes mainly from Veneto, including Conegliano-Valdobbiadene.
slides.23.questions.3.question: What is the core grape of Soave DOC?
slides.23.questions.3.explanation: Soave’s core grape is Garganega (at least 70%), which may be blended with Trebbiano di Soave and/or Chardonnay; it is the same variety as Sicilia’s Grecanico Dorato.
slides.23.questions.4.question: Which wines are made in the Valpolicella area? (multiple choice)
slides.23.questions.4.options.0: A. Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG (dried grapes)
slides.23.questions.4.explanation: Valpolicella has four official appellations: Valpolicella DOC, Valpolicella Ripasso DOC, Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG and Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG. Barolo is in Piemonte.
slides.23.questions.5.question: What category is Soave Classico?
slides.23.questions.5.explanation: Soave Classico is the historic core sub-zone of Soave DOC; the stricter Soave Superiore and the sweet Recioto di Soave are DOCGs.
slides.23.questions.6.question: What is the minimum ageing for Amarone della Valpolicella?
slides.23.questions.6.explanation: Amarone needs at least 14% ABV and 2 years’ ageing; Riserva at least 4 years.
slides.23.questions.7.question: DNA has shown Garganega to be identical to which grape?
slides.23.questions.7.explanation: Garganega is the same variety as Sicilia’s Grecanico Dorato; Trebbiano di Soave, meanwhile, is identical to Marche’s Verdicchio.
slides.23.questions.8.question: What is Bardolino Chiaretto?
slides.23.questions.8.options.1: B. A rosé made with brief skin contact
slides.23.questions.8.options.2: C. A traditional method sparkling white
slides.23.questions.8.options.3: D. A red from dried grapes
slides.23.questions.8.explanation: Bardolino Chiaretto is a rosé made with brief skin contact, considered one of Italy’s best rosatos.
slides.23.questions.9.question: Which estate revived the ripasso technique in the 1960s?
slides.23.questions.9.explanation: Ripasso is an old Valpolicella tradition revived by Masi in the 1960s: fresh Valpolicella is steeped on Amarone/Recioto pomace for 1-2 weeks, triggering a brief second fermentation.
